title: Early psychosis detection and intervention
bottleneck: Schizophrenia is typically diagnosed years after onset, after psychosis has damaged education, employment, and brain structure, yet prodromal symptoms are nonspecific and most at-risk youth never convert, making early intervention ethically and practically fraught. No biomarker reliably identifies who will develop psychosis.
why_it_blocks: Duration of untreated psychosis predicts worse long-term outcomes, so every year of diagnostic delay is permanent disability. The field cannot intervene early because it cannot predict.
current_state: Clinical high-risk criteria and early-intervention services modestly improve outcomes. Omega-3, CBT, and low-dose antipsychotic prevention trials show mixed results; neuroimaging and speech-pattern biomarkers are experimental. Speech-pattern analysis and smartphone-based monitoring can flag prodromal changes in research cohorts, yet false-positive rates make population screening ethically fraught. Until prediction improves, indicated prevention will remain limited to the small fraction of at-risk youth who reach specialty clinics.
